title: Spacecraft beyond Earth
what: Every craft sent beyond Earth orbit, from Luna 1 in 1959 to today, where it was at the moment shown, and those that set out but never left. With them, the Hubble Space Telescope, which stays in orbit about Earth.
how: The record is Jonathan McDowell’s GCAT: each craft that left Earth orbit (not its rocket stages), with each stretch of its flight about one body, and its landing; NASA NSSDCA’s chronology gives each mission’s objective and outcome, and the craft that set out but never left (failures at launch, probes stranded in Earth orbit). Paths are JPL Horizons’s where it has the craft (about 104), thinned to as few points as draw them within 75,000 km about the Sun, 1,000 km through a flyby, 500 km near Earth; a long stay in orbit is drawn at its world. For the others the path is approximate, drawn amber: each leg as the transfer orbit between where it left and where it arrived, as first planned, not as flown; within about 0.02 AU of Horizons for a direct transfer. A leg to a comet or asteroid, or one that loops back to the world it left, is not drawn. The Hubble Space Telescope never left Earth orbit: it is there by name, from GCAT’s satellite catalogue, drawn when Earth is close up as a circle 611 to 620 km up, tilted 28.47° to the equator, as its orbit was first measured in May 1990, gone round in 97 minutes. Where it is along the circle and which way the circle faces are not its true ones, and it has sunk and been lifted since: it too is drawn amber. Webb’s card shows it in 3D, a model built here from NASA’s published sizes, at true scale: an approximation, not a copy of any published model; Hubble’s card shows its own, built the same way from ESA/Hubble’s sizes (13.2 m long, 4.2 m across, two solar arrays each 2.45 m by 7.56 m). Its mirror is 18 gold hexagons on one curve, its secondary on three struts, its sunshield five layers opening apart toward their edges; the bus, solar array and antenna below are placed by eye from NASA’s pictures. The Sun is drawn below, where the sunshield always faces it; a light from the viewer’s side shows the mirror, which in space is always in shade. Its card also goes to it: the camera then orbits the model where Webb is at the moment shown, at true size and lit by the Sun from its true direction, with Earth, the Moon and the Sun where they are from it. It is drawn with its sunshield to the Sun, as it always is, and its mirror turned toward the celestial north, a convention: where it looks at a given moment is not known here. It is drawn where Horizons has it, on its halo orbit about L2, hundreds of thousands of km across; craft at L2 that Horizons does not have are drawn at the point itself. Hubble’s card goes to it too, about Earth, 615 km up, Earth filling half the sky below: drawn with its solar arrays square to the Sun and its aperture turned toward the celestial north, a convention, as where it is looking at a given moment is not known here; it is never pointed near the Sun.
